ab337a3ebbac: How it came about: Bill W.'s "Money" (1946)
7a2cf50a302d: <0>At first there was no money to argue about.</0> Members met in homes, and if one wanted to help another alcoholic financially, that was his own affair (P-17, p. 27). Bill accepts that this couldn't last: meeting places, clubs and offices cost money, so the real question was how to limit money so that it never topples the spiritual foundation (P-17, pp. 27–28).
8a631d0df6c0: <0>Members' contributions keep the services honest.</0> Contributions are never a condition of membership (P-17, p. 28). Because nobody is compelled to pay, A.A.'s offices "can never dictate" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 29): if they serve badly, members stop paying. That is why members' own voluntary contributions should be "eventually our sole support" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 32).
c2fa15809939: <0>A.A. did take outside help once, and says so.</0> There was a time "when we desperately needed a little outside aid" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 33). Friends' gifts made possible the Alcoholic Foundation, the book <1>Alcoholics Anonymous</1> and the General Office, and Bill writes that A.A. would never stop being grateful (P-17, p. 33).
ed0a1c4ee894: <0>Why that changed.</0> By 1946 A.A. had thousands of members earning a living, and a strong feeling spread that A.A. should support itself (P-17, p. 33). Let the public's money go to research, hospitals and education, which need it; "We can, and we should, pay our own way" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34).
cda0b6d524f6: <0>What counts and what doesn't.</0> A nonalcoholic friend dropping a dollar in the hat is hardly an exception to self-support (P-17, p. 34). The concern is "the large contributions, especially those that may carry future obligations" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34), and money left to A.A. in wills, public solicitation in A.A.'s name, and money from "wet" or "dry" sources, which would drag A.A. into the alcohol controversy (P-17, p. 34). Bill even questions a large gift from a wealthy member: might the group feel in his debt, and might he think he had bought his sobriety (P-17, p. 34)? His conclusion is that "acceptance of large donations from any source whatever is very questionable" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34).
017cc2f198b3: <0>The trustees' decision.</0> Bill reports that the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation had just resolved to turn down any gift carrying the slightest obligation and any earnings offered from a commercial source, including money from film companies interested in an A.A. film, because "A.A. has nothing to sell" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 35).

a2081b185585: The Ninth Tradition's Long Form walks through A.A.'s structure from the bottom up:
136edeec8f66: Bill W., "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947)
4a3588281d2b: <0>His answer.</0> "The answer to this question is almost surely" no, and he says experience has settled it (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37).
509517ff35e0: <0>Why.</0> Alcoholics could rarely govern themselves, and families, doctors, clergy and judges had failed to govern them by force (P-17, p. 37). But alcoholics can be led and inspired, so the only real authority in A.A. is spiritual principle: "It is never personal authority" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37). He lists what A.A. lacks: no fees, no dues, no rules, no demand that anyone conform, "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37).
181089843f2f: <0>Why groups follow the Traditions anyway.</0> Members follow the Steps by choice, because they prefer recovery to death: "We conform because we want to" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). Groups follow the Twelve Points of Tradition for the same reason: they see they would fall apart if they didn't (P-17, p. 38).
0f1d8574117d: <0>No one can compel a group.</0> There is no constituted "human authority that can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). An elected leader can guide by example or persuasion but can never boss, or he is passed over at the next election (P-17, p. 38). Rotating committees "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38); each carries out what it thinks its group wants. Committees that tried to discipline members or police their morals achieved nothing lasting, except perhaps getting a new committee elected (P-17, p. 38).
a7c49dbc4f2c: <0>Bill's own attempt.</0> He tried to govern A.A. himself, and each time "I have been shouted down" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39). Personal power always failed, and he concluded that in A.A. "one can be a servant only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39).
200b1dca171c: <0>The center is a center of service.</0> The General Office supplies information and literature, helps new groups when asked, looks after public relations and sometimes mediates (P-17, p. 39). The Grapevine's editors see themselves as a mirror of A.A., unable to rule or propagandize, and the trustees are "caretakers only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39). Even at the center there are only custodians, editors and secretaries, none with authority to govern A.A. (P-17, p. 39). So long as A.A. avoids piling up wealth or personal government at these centers, he writes, it can't go astray (P-17, pp. 39–40).
0d0cd80f9e25: It settles that no person, committee, office or board in A.A. has authority over a group or a member. It doesn't say A.A. has no structure: the Long Form names the structure and explains whom it answers to. For how a group's own decisions are reached, see <0>Is group conscience a majority vote?</0> and <1>Tradition Two: does anyone have authority in A.A.?</1>

In 1937, at Dr. Bob's home in Akron, the two men added up two years' work and saw for the first time that recovery on a large scale was possible (P-44). The question was how a few recovered alcoholics could reach millions (P-44). They met with eighteen members of the Akron group; the majority wanted hospitals, paid workers and, above all, "a book for other alcoholics that could explain to them our methods and results" (P-44). The big money never came: John D. Rockefeller, Jr. gave $5,000 but declined to give more "for fear of professionalizing A.A." (P-44). 3417efd60a23: How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)?
b922fc912849: In 1938 the publisher Harper offered Bill W. an advance for the book. He and his partner Hank P. decided the fellowship should own its own book, and instead formed their own company, Works Publishing, selling $25 shares to members and friends.
b9ba80d96af7: They sold 200 shares for $5,000, mostly in monthly installments, after a Reader's Digest editor seemed to promise an article. A loan from Charles B. Towns, owner of the hospital where Bill got sober, helped too. Cornwall Press printed 5,000 copies for a $500 down payment, and the book came out in April 1939 at $3.50.
b340eb874e16: The Digest article never came, and for months the book didn't sell. Publicity in 1939 and 1940 finally moved it.
58f5dcd63834: In 1940 the Alcoholic Foundation bought out the cash shareholders with money lent by Rockefeller and his friends, and Bill and Hank gave up their shares, so the Big Book came to belong to A.A. as a whole.
fa2ed05fe98c: The decision to self-publish (1957, and P-44)
d60f85133141: In the fall of 1938, through trustee Frank Amos, Bill showed two chapters to Eugene Exman, religious editor at Harper, who offered a $1,500 advance on royalties (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill had second thoughts: if the book became the fellowship's main text, "Our principal written asset would then be owned by an outside publisher" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The trustees favored Harper, but Hank P. pressed for a stock company of their own (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Exman himself agreed that a society like theirs should publish its own literature (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 (Bill, describing events through 1955) puts the reason plainly: "No publisher, however good, ought to own our best asset." (P-44).
403efde29c4f: Hank's prospectus offered 600 shares at $25: a third for cash to New York members and friends, two-thirds to Hank and Bill for their work, with the author's royalty assigned to the Foundation to soothe the trustees (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He named the company "Since the forthcoming volume would be only the first of many such 'works,'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and bought blank stock certificates at a stationery store (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
c08a63c6d858: At first nobody bought: "What made you think that we would buy stock in a book not yet written?" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then the managing editor of the Reader's Digest said he was almost sure the magazine would run a story when the book was ready (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). With that, "Soon we had a subscription of 200 shares which amounted to $5,000" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), paid in installments of five dollars a month (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Charles B. Towns lent $2,500 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), a sum Bill elsewhere says later grew to over $4,000 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The money went for office costs and groceries for Bill, Lois, Hank and the secretary, Ruth Hock, until publication (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
29b7ae92d4a6: Edward Blackwell of Cornwall Press suggested a first printing of 5,000 and accepted $500 down (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). They set the price at $3.50 after heated argument, and to give buyers their money's worth used the thickest paper in the shop: "The original volume proved to be so bulky that it became known as the 'Big Book.'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
aa05009e96bb: When Bill and Hank went back to the Reader's Digest, the editor had forgotten them; his staff had turned the idea down (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "The book enterprise had collapsed." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Twenty-eight copies were owed to the story writers and forty-nine to subscribers (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Blackwell stood by them (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A radio appearance and 20,000 postcards to doctors brought two orders (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). An A.A. tailor, Bert T., borrowed $1,000 against his own business to keep the company going (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Sales began with a Liberty magazine article in September 1939 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and grew after Rockefeller's dinner in 1940 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>Why did early A.A. turn down Rockefeller money?</0>
8093e8100431: How A.A. came to own it
9969317b1a83: By 1940 some cash subscribers wanted their money back (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Trustee A. LeRoy Chipman borrowed $8,000 from Rockefeller, two of his sons and dinner guests to buy their shares at par, to be repaid from book profits (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill turned his 200 shares over to the Foundation; Hank, then drinking, agreed only when the Foundation paid him $200 for office furniture he owned (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "And that is how the society of Alcoholics Anonymous, through its Trustees, came to own the Big Book." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 adds that two years later the book had done so well that the loan was paid off (P-44).
2ee9a22d6c09: <0>Hank's shares.</0> P-44 says "Hank P. and I donated our shares in it to the Alcoholic Foundation" (P-44). Bill's 1957 book and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) say Hank resisted and gave his up for a $200 payment for furniture (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Pass It On, 1984).
ea82004b1e2b: <0>The company's name.</0> Bill (1957) says Hank chose "Works" because the book would be the first of many works (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> calls it "a matter of some dispute": some said it came from Anne Smith's favorite verse, "Faith without works is dead"; "others said it was named for a favorite slogan of the membership" (Pass It On, 1984), "It works!"
10b7575d4ea0: <0>The Towns loan.</0> $2,500 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; P-44), or "later increased to over $4,000" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
7875bab723d2: <0>Who was responsible.</0> <1>Pass It On</1> reports Hank's son's view that Hank got the project rolling, and Ruth Hock's that the two were about equally responsible: without Bill it wouldn't have been written, and "it wouldn't have been published without Hank" (Pass It On, 1984).
